guideTitle: Best Bread Makers With Yogurt Function (2026)
metaTitle: Best Bread Makers With Yogurt Function (2026)
metaDescription: Six bread makers with a yogurt program compared on temperature control, pan material, capacity and extra cycles, so one machine covers loaves and cultures.
expertTake: The KBS Pro 24-in-1 is the best pick because its yogurt program sits beside a ceramic pan, dual-heater convection and two custom slots. The Neretva 20-in-1 is the value pick. Anyone who wants yogurt as a daily staple should skip a bread maker and buy a dedicated yogurt maker with jars.
introParagraphs: A yogurt cycle on a bread maker looks like a free bonus, and it can be a useful one. Yogurt needs a long, gentle, steady warmth, which is exactly what a bread machine's low heat setting can provide when it is programmed for it.

The details decide whether it works. Pan material, how well the chamber holds temperature and whether you can cover the pan matter more than the label on the button. This guide explains how the function works and which machines make it practical.

products.name: KBS Pro 2.2LB 24-in-1 Dual-Heater Bread Maker
products.description:
The KBS Pro lists yogurt among twenty-four automatic menus, alongside sourdough, pasta dough and pizza dough. That breadth makes it the most capable machine here, and two homemade menus let you adjust a yogurt schedule if the preset does not suit your starter. A 2.2-pound capacity and a ceramic pan with automatic nut dispenser round out the package.

For yogurt the details matter. The convection heater system is designed to circulate warm air around the pan, which can keep the chamber at a more even temperature than a single bottom element. Against the KBS Blue, the Pro offers more programs and custom slots but no touchscreen, and against the Neretva it has more power and more flexibility at a higher cost.

Ownership notes: clean the pan thoroughly with hot water before yogurt, because leftover dough residue or soap can interfere with the culture. Dedicate a pan or a lined container to yogurt if you can, and wipe the chamber after each batch.
products.bestFor: Bakers who want a flexible yogurt cycle with custom time control.
pros: Twenty-four menus including yogurt, sourdough and pasta dough
Two homemade menus to tune a yogurt schedule
Dual-heater convection for steadier chamber temperature
Ceramic pan with automatic nut dispenser
cons: Costs more than basic yogurt-capable machines
Large menu takes time to learn
Pan is large for small yogurt batches

products.name: Neretva 20-in-1 2LB Bread Machine With Dual Heater and Yogurt Cycle
products.description:
The Neretva 20-in-1 covers yogurt as one of its twenty customized menus, together with jam, cake, dough and gluten-free. The pan is a nonstick ceramic one, a sensible match for yogurt, since a smooth coating is easier to sanitize than a scratched metal pan. A two-pound capacity suits a household of two to four.

The appeal is a balance of cost and function. Dual heaters with 360-degree heat and a 550W rating give steady warmth, and a power-recovery feature protects a long culture from a short outage, which matters because a yogurt batch that cools below the culture range stalls. Against the KBS Pro, it has fewer programs and no custom slots, and against the SUMSATY it offers a more established brand.

Practical care is simple. Scald the pan with hot water before use, keep the lid closed during the culture and let the batch chill in the fridge before stirring. Wash with a soft sponge to protect the ceramic. Because the pan is large, many owners line it with a clean food-safe container or ladle the milk into jars set inside the chamber, which keeps the bread pan free of dairy residue.
products.bestFor: Households that want occasional yogurt from a mid-priced machine.
pros: Ceramic pan is easy to sanitize
Power interruption recovery protects long cultures
cons: 550W is modest for dense bread doughs
Large pan is awkward for small yogurt batches

products.name: KBS Blue 2.2LB Smart Bread Maker With Touchscreen
products.description:
The KBS Blue puts yogurt and jam on a shared program in a seventeen-program list, with fifty-three chef-created recipes to guide you. A touchscreen makes the options clear, and a 710W motor handles bread doughs. It is aimed at someone who wants guidance rather than a blank panel.

For yogurt, the recipes are the value. A first-time maker often misjudges milk temperature or culture time, and a guided recipe helps. Against the KBS Pro, the Blue has fewer programs but a friendlier interface, and against the Neretva it offers recipe support and a stronger motor. A fifteen-hour delay timer is useful for bread but should not be used with fresh milk and starter in a warm room.

Ownership centers on the touchscreen and the pan. Keep the screen dry, wipe it with a soft cloth and use the ceramic pan with care. If the screen fails, the machine is limited, so check the warranty length. The guided yogurt recipes are a useful way to learn the right temperatures, and after a few batches most owners can make yogurt without looking at the screen.
products.bestFor: New yogurt makers who want guided recipes.
cons: Fewer programs than the KBS Pro
Touchscreen is another part that can fail
Delay timer is unsuitable for fresh milk cultures

products.name: Rosewill 25-in-1 Automatic Bread Maker With 700W Heaters
products.description:
The Rosewill lists twenty-five programs including gluten-free, cake, yogurt and jam, and gives you three crust colors and three loaf sizes up to two pounds. Its 700W heaters at the top and bottom are designed for a 360-degree bake, which also helps hold the chamber at a steady low temperature in a yogurt cycle.

The key practical feature for yogurt is the power-recovery system. A forty-minute recovery window means a brief outage will not wreck a six to ten hour culture, though a longer cut will. Against the KBS Pro, the Rosewill has less control over custom schedules but a simpler panel, and against the Neretva it offers more programs and a bit more power.

In practice, treat the yogurt program as a long, quiet job. Use a clean pan, keep the lid closed and avoid opening the machine during the culture. Wipe the chamber afterward to remove milk splatter, which can sour and smell. Yogurt rarely splatters, but a boiled-over milk step beforehand can leave film on the elements.
products.bestFor: Bakers who want many programs and a recovery feature.
pros: Three crust colors and loaf sizes
cons: Large pan is awkward for small batches

products.name: SUMSATY 2.2LB 16-in-1 Bread Maker With Yogurt
products.description:
The SUMSATY offers sixteen customizable programs, with dedicated modes for jam, yogurt and a homemade setting for your own recipes. A 2.2-pound capacity, 600W power and a quoted noise level under 50 dB aim it at households that bake in the evening. The homemade setting is useful for yogurt because it lets you set your own temperature hold and time.

Its selling point is a compact, quiet-leaning design with a basic yogurt cycle. Against the KBS Pro, it has fewer programs and less power, and against the KOVIET it lacks dual dispensers but includes the homemade slot. A modest 600W motor handles standard doughs but may labor on heavy whole grain loaves.

Ownership is routine. Hand wash the pan, keep the lid clean and check the manual for the yogurt temperature range. If you plan to make yogurt often, consider buying a second pan so one stays reserved for it.
products.bestFor: Evening bakers who want quiet operation and a basic yogurt cycle.
cons: 600W motor is modest for dense doughs
Fewer programs than the larger machines
Noise claim is the maker's own figure

products.name: KOVIET 25-in-1 2LB Bread Maker With Dual Dispensers
products.description:
The KOVIET combines twenty-five baking options, including a yogurt setting, with individual dual dispensers that release ingredients at the right moment under adaptive temperature control. A thickened stainless steel body, a thirteen-hour delay timer and one-hour keep-warm complete the specification.

Adaptive temperature control is relevant to yogurt, since the culture needs a steady range rather than a roaring bake. Against the Rosewill, the KOVIET adds dispensers and a sturdier body, and against the KBS Pro it lacks the ceramic pan and custom slots. A two-pound capacity suits a household of two to four.

Care is the usual routine. Hand wash the pan, wipe the dispensers and chamber and let everything dry. For yogurt, use the pan only with food-safe, unscented cleaners and rinse thoroughly.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want dispensers and a yogurt setting in one machine.
pros: Twenty-five options including a yogurt setting
Dual dispensers with adaptive temperature control
cons: Standard nonstick pan rather than ceramic

buyingCriteria.criterion: How a bread machine makes yogurt
buyingCriteria.explanation: Yogurt culture needs a steady warmth of about 40 to 45 C for six to twelve hours, which is far below baking temperatures. A bread machine's yogurt program holds the chamber at a low heat for that long, while the pan holds the milk and starter. The method works, but the pan is large, so a small batch may not warm evenly, and a full pan of milk uses a lot of dairy. The usual routine is to heat the milk to about 82 C to denature the proteins, cool it to roughly 43 C, stir in a spoonful of live culture and start the program. Skipping the cooling step is the commonest way to kill a culture, so use a thermometer rather than guessing by touch.

Culture dies above roughly 50 C and stalls below about 35 C, so stable heat matters. Dual-heater convection systems like the KBS Pro's circulate air for a steadier chamber, while a single element can create hot and cool spots. Check the manual's stated range, and measure the milk temperature once before you rely on the program. A cheap probe thermometer dropped into the pan after an hour tells you whether the hold is nearer 38 C or 45 C, and that single reading explains why one machine makes thick, mild yogurt while another makes thin, tart batches from the same recipe.

A ceramic pan, as on the KBS Pro and Neretva, is smooth and easy to scald clean. A scratched nonstick pan can harbor residue that interferes with culture. Scald the pan with boiling water before each batch, and avoid pans with dough residue stuck in the paddle well.

The KBS Pro's two homemade menus and the SUMSATY's homemade setting let you adjust culture time, which matters because different starters and milks take different hours. A fixed preset may run too long and make the yogurt sour. Machines without custom control force you to stop the cycle manually. Longer culture times make tangier yogurt, because the bacteria keep converting lactose into lactic acid, so a six-hour batch is milder and a twelve-hour batch is sharp. Whole milk gives a thicker set than skim, and a spoonful of milk powder can firm up a thin batch.

Never use a delay timer with fresh milk and starter in a warm kitchen, since the mixture can spoil before the culture starts. The yogurt program should start at once, not hours later. Delay timers are for bread, not for dairy. The same caution applies to the keep-warm feature, which holds the chamber at a baking-adjacent temperature that will overheat and curdle a finished yogurt. When the culture time ends, move the pan to the refrigerator so the yogurt chills and firms up.

A bread pan holds around two liters, so each batch is big. If you eat a small amount of yogurt, a bread machine yields more than you can finish, and a dedicated yogurt maker with jars suits small households better. Think about whether you will really use the yogurt function monthly or only once. If you do commit, pour the yogurt into jars after chilling rather than storing it in the pan, and keep a portion as the starter for the next batch to avoid buying culture each time.

howWeEvaluated.title: Yogurt capability
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated whether each machine lists a yogurt program and gives control over it. The KBS Pro and SUMSATY add custom or homemade slots, while the Rosewill and Neretva offer presets with power recovery.

howWeEvaluated.title: Temperature steadiness
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered heater layout and chamber design. Dual-heater convection on the KBS Pro and 360-degree heat on the Neretva should hold a low temperature more evenly than a single element.

howWeEvaluated.title: Pan and sanitation
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at pan material. Ceramic pans on the KBS and Neretva machines are easier to sanitize than scratched nonstick, which matters for a culture.

howWeEvaluated.title: Bread performance
howWeEvaluated.description: A bread machine must still bake bread well. We weighed motor power, with the KBS Blue's 710W and Rosewill's 700W heaters against the SUMSATY's 600W.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ease of use
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared controls, from the KBS Blue's touchscreen and recipes to plain panels. A guided recipe helps first-time yogurt makers.

rows: Yogurt cycle with power recovery at a mid price

cards.label: Preset
cards.text: The Rosewill, Neretva and KOVIET offer a fixed yogurt program. It is simple and works with typical recipes, but gives little control over sourness.

cards.label: Custom
cards.text: The KBS Pro and SUMSATY let you set your own schedule, which helps tune sourness and thickness. It takes a few batches to dial in.

howToChoose.note: Pick preset for simplicity; pick custom if you want control.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A stable low hold, a clean pan and a way to avoid opening the lid during the culture. Use a thermometer once to confirm the machine's real temperature. Keep the first batch small and plain, with whole milk and a store-bought live culture, so you know the baseline before experimenting with flavors.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The KBS Pro gives the most control, the Neretva is the practical middle and the SUMSATY is the budget route to a homemade slot.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You bake bread weekly and also want yogurt. The KBS Pro or KBS Blue gives better control and a stronger motor.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Yogurt is an occasional experiment. The SUMSATY or Neretva covers it.

maintenance.why: Residue interferes with culture. Rinse with boiling water to sanitize.
Milk splatter sours and smells. Wipe with a damp cloth when cool.
Dishwashers wear coatings. Use a soft sponge and unscented soap.
A thermometer confirms the real hold temperature before you trust a preset.
A worn paddle shaft can leak dough or milk. Replace it if it wobbles.

faq.q: Can a bread maker really make yogurt?
faq.a: Yes, if it has a yogurt program that holds a low, steady heat of about 40 to 45 C. The method works, though the large pan makes big batches.

faq.q: Which bread maker is best for yogurt?
faq.a: The KBS Pro 24-in-1 gives the most control with two homemade menus and a ceramic pan. The Neretva 20-in-1 is a simpler, lower-cost route.

faq.q: Do I need a starter culture?
faq.a: Yes. Use a few tablespoons of plain live-culture yogurt or a freeze-dried starter, then warm the milk to the temperature the recipe calls for before adding it.

faq.q: Is it better to use a yogurt maker?
faq.a: For small, frequent batches, yes, since jars are more convenient. A bread machine suits people who want one appliance for both jobs.

faq.q: Can I use the delay timer for yogurt?
faq.a: No. Fresh milk and starter can spoil if left for hours. Start the yogurt program right away.

faq.q: Why did my yogurt come out runny?
faq.a: Usually the temperature drifted outside the culture range, the milk was added to the culture while too hot or the batch ran too short. Ultra-pasteurized milk can also set weakly, so try a regular pasteurized brand. Check the machine's hold temperature and add time in a custom slot.
